title: SpaceX Launches Starlink Satellites from California as Falcon 9 Cadence Slows (Photos)
body:
SpaceX lifted off a fresh batch of Starlink broadband satellites from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California on Tuesday, marking another step in the company’s effort to expand its global internet constellation even as the launch cadence of its workhorse Falcon 9 rockets begins to decelerate. The mission, designated Starlink‑31, placed 46 next‑generation satellites into low‑Earth orbit, bringing the total number of operational Starlink units to more than 4,000 and reinforcing the network’s coverage over the Pacific and the Americas. While the launch itself proceeded without incident, industry observers see the slower rhythm of Falcon 9 flights as a sign that SpaceX is transitioning its focus toward the next phase of its launch strategy: the fully reusable Starship system.

The Vandenberg launch was notable for several technical upgrades. The payload consisted of the newer “v2.0” satellites, which feature larger phased‑array antennas and higher‑throughput Ka‑band transponders, promising faster speeds and lower latency for users in remote regions. In addition, SpaceX employed a modified version of its “rideshare” configuration, bundling the Starlink payload with a small secondary payload—a CubeSat for a university research program—demonstrating the company’s continued commitment to supporting scientific and educational missions alongside its commercial objectives.

Historically, SpaceX has been able to sustain a near‑daily launch cadence from its Florida and California pads, a tempo that has been instrumental in rapidly populating the Starlink constellation. However, in recent months the frequency of Falcon 9 missions has tapered, with several weeks passing between launches. Analysts attribute this slowdown to a combination of factors: the completion of the primary phase of the Starlink rollout, the need to allocate launch resources to other high‑profile customers such as NASA and the U.S. Department of Defense, and, most critically, the intensive testing regime surrounding Starship. The massive, fully reusable launch vehicle, still in its prototype stage, demands significant engineering manpower and launch‑pad availability, prompting SpaceX to prioritize its development over the more routine Falcon 9 schedule.

The shift has broader implications for the satellite‑internet market. Competitors such as OneWeb and Amazon’s Project Kuiper are also racing to deploy their own constellations, and the ability to launch large numbers of satellites quickly has been a competitive edge for SpaceX. A reduced Falcon 9 cadence could give rivals a window to close the gap, especially if Starship’s inaugural orbital flights encounter setbacks. Nonetheless, SpaceX executives remain confident that Starship will ultimately deliver a dramatic increase in payload capacity—up to 100 tonnes per launch—allowing the company to replenish and expand its satellite fleet in far fewer missions than currently required.

Looking ahead, the Vandenberg launch underscores a transitional moment for SpaceX. The company appears to be deliberately winding down the high‑frequency Falcon 9 schedule to free up resources for Starship’s development, test flights, and eventual operational deployment. If Starship achieves its projected performance and reliability, SpaceX could usher in an era where entire constellations are launched in a handful of missions, slashing costs and turnaround times. Until then, the incremental additions of newer Starlink satellites will continue to enhance service quality for existing users while the aerospace community watches closely for the next milestone in SpaceX’s ambitious launch roadmap.
